Selby's population increased by around 8,500 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 92,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Selby increased by 10.2%, from just over 83,400 in 2011 to around 92,000 in 2021.

This means Selby's population saw the largest percentage increase in Yorkshire and The Humber. The population of Yorkshire and The Humber increased by 3.7%, while the population of England rose by 6.6%.

In 2021, Selby was home to around 1.1 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.0 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 15% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Selby than across Yorkshire and The Humber

An older Selby

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Selby increased by two years, from 42 to 44 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than Yorkshire and The Humber as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 2,900 (an increase of 37.1%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just under 2,000 (10.3% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 2.3 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Family in Selby

Selby saw Yorkshire and The Humber's largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of households including a couple with only non-dependent children (from 7.3% in 2011 to 6.7% in 2021).

Doncaster saw Yorkshire and The Humber's next largest decrease in the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children (from 7.1% in 2011 to 6.6% in 2021).

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children remained 6.0%, while the percentage in nearby East Riding of Yorkshire fell from 6.7% to 6.3%.

The percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children in Selby decreased by 0.6 percentage points

Religion in Selby

In 2021, 38.8% of Selby residents reported having "No religion", up from 21.7% in 2011. The rise of 17.2 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Selby. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 25.9% to 39.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 54.7% of people in Selby described themselves as Christian (down from 70.9%), while 5.3% did not state their religion (down from 6.7% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 38.8% of usual residents in Selby reported having "No religion"

Rise in private renting

In 2021, 13.4% of Selby households rented privately. This figure increased from 11.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in eight households (12.3%) lived in socially rented housing, compared with 12.0% in 2011. The percentage of Selby households that owned their home (outright or with a mortgage or loan) decreased from 75.0% to 73.1%.

This area had the region’s lowest percentage of privately-rented homes. Wakefield had Yorkshire and The Humber's next lowest percentage of privately-rented homes (14.9%), while Kingston upon Hull had the region's highest percentage (23.9%).

Private renting in Selby increased by 2.4 percentage points

Unpaid care in Selby

In 2021, 4.5% of Selby residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.3% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, 1.6% of residents (aged five years and over) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.3% in 2011. The proportion of Selby residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care increased from 2.3% to 2.5%.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Selby (2.8 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across Yorkshire and The Humber (2.7 percentage points, from 7.1% to 4.4%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Selby decreased by 2.8 percentage points

Selby residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 84,600 Selby residents said they were born in England. This represented 92.0% of the local population. The figure has risen from just over 77,600 in 2011, which at the time represented 93.0% of Selby's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just over 1,400 Selby residents reporting this country of birth (1.6%). This figure was down from around 1,500 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.7% of the population of Selby.

The number of Selby residents born in Poland rose from just under 950 in 2011 (1.1% of the local population) to just over 1,400 in 2021 (1.6%).

In 2021, 92.0% of Selby residents reported their country of birth as England

People looking after their family or home in Selby

In 2021, 3.4% of Selby residents (aged 16 years and over) said they were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (3.2%).

The percentage of people who were economically inactive because they were looking after their family or home increased from 3.9% to 4.9% across Yorkshire and The Humber. Across England, the percentage increased from 4.0% to 4.8%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were looking after their family or home (economically inactive) in Selby increased by 0.2 percentage points

Working hours in Selby

In 2021, 9.1% of Selby residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (9.0%).

In 2021, just over one in eight people (12.6%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 14.8% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 57.1% to 59.8%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week was 9.7% (similar to 2011) across Yorkshire and The Humber. Across England, the percentage increased from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Selby increased by 0.1 percentage points

National identity in Selby

In 2021, 3.4% of Selby residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 2.7% in 2011.

In 2021, 0.9% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.3% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Selby that identified as "British only" increased from 14.2% to 58.7%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.6 percentage points, from 5.1% to 6.7%) than in Selby (0.7 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Selby increased by 0.7 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Selby residents aged 16 years and over, 30.3% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 26.5% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in two people (51.8%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 55.5% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Selby that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 8.9% to 9.6%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership in Selby (3.7 percentage points) was similar to the increase across Yorkshire and The Humber (3.8 percentage points, from 33.9% to 37.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Selby increased by 3.7 percentage points

Disability in Selby

In 2021, 6.2% of Selby residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 7.8% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.9%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 9.6% in 2011. The proportion of Selby residents who were not disabled increased from 82.6% to 83.9%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Selby (1.6 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.7 percentage points, from 9.9% to 8.2%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Selby decreased by 1.6 percentage points

Health in Selby

In 2021, 49.3% of Selby residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 47.5% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" rose from 34.3% to 34.4%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Selby residents describing their health as "very bad" was 0.9% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 3.8% to 3.3%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Selby increased by 1.8 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Selby

In 2021, 0.4% of Selby residents identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group"), up from 0.0% in 2011. The 0.3 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of people from the "Other ethnic groups" ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.8% to 1.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 1.0% to 2.2%.

In 2021, 97.7% of people in Selby identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 98.4% in 2011), while 1.0% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.8% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category increased from 0.6% in 2011 to 0.8% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
